text:
maria: Quick summary from today's QA runs — posting notes and questions.
jen: nice, drop the numbers pls and any weird regressions.
kai: ran replay harness against prod traces (24h) and a synthetic burst profile. keeping kernels constant (f32->q8) to isolate batching.
liam: solid. did you pin kernel variants in the runtime config or override at request time?
kai: pinned via kernel_override in the test config so scheduling didn't swap kernels mid-run.
sasha: TL:DR: TTFT moved ~10% on the synthetic burst for long-context (>1024) flows. p95 shifted more than p99 though.
maria: can we break down TTFT vs TPOT? I want to be clear on definitions for the writeup.
jen: my notes: TTFT = time from request acceptance to first token emitted by the runtime (includes queuing + kernel setup + first kernel exec). TPOT = time per output token, measured as average inter-token latency after streaming starts (so excludes queuing for first token but includes runtime token emission cost).
liam: add: for batched workloads TPOT is strongly affected by batch size and KV cache hit rate.
kai: yep. in replay runs where cache warmed, goodput rose 2.3x vs cold-cache. QPS stayed same but useful tokens/sec increased.
sasha: that matches the hypothesis: goodput != QPS. QPS counts requests, goodput counts tokens successfully emitted per second (or effective tokens/sec after dedup/dropped outputs).
maria: request: for the doc let's include these concrete metrics: TTFT (median/p95/p99), TPOT (avg + 98th percentile), goodput (tokens/sec), and effective throughput (concurrent requests * avg tokens/request / wall time).
jen: agree. and add a breakdown column for "kernel wait" vs "batch formation" vs "kv lookup" vs "compute".
kai: I have a short profiler snippet that shows time slices — pasting minimal example:

[RUN] req=0x7f1a kernel_wait=12ms batch_form=8ms kv_lookup=2ms compute=45ms first_emit=67ms
[RUN] req=0x7f2b kernel_wait=4ms batch_form=22ms kv_lookup=1ms compute=40ms first_emit=67ms

liam: neat, the first_emit calc matches TTFT definition.
sasha: one anomaly: in the synthetic burst the batch_form time jumped to 60ms intermittently causing p95 TTFT spikes. looks like our batching heuristic threshold/rate limiter interplay.
kai: I instrumented the batching code — the heuristic triggers flush when either size limit or latency threshold reached. the burst produced many small requests that hit size limit rarely, so flush-on-latency kept them in a timer wheel. timer delays were uneven.
maria: is that an OS scheduling issue on the node or our event loop timer implementation?
jen: likely event-loop/timer batching interaction. we saw similar in the past where timer drift caused correlated flushes.
liam: mitigation options: lower latency threshold (better TTFT but worse TPOT), increase aggressiveness for small-req bursts, or enable tiny-request fast-path that bypasses batching.
sasha: fast-path seems promising for CX use-cases (short prompts). but costs increase in compute overhead. we should quantify cost impact in Optimize.
kai: Also KV cache behavior: replay runs show cache hit ratio variation across users. For models with long contexts the KV cache hit-rate matters a lot for TPOT. Example: cold-cache TPOT=80ms, warm-cache TPOT=45ms.
maria: action items: 1) collect per-run histogram of batch sizes, timer delays, and kernel queue depth. 2) reproduce timer-flush correlation on a smaller node locally. 3) draft definition section for TTFT/TPOT/goodput for the benchmarks doc.
jen: I'll take item 1.
kai: i'll do 2 and dump the local trace.
sasha: I'll write the metric defs and send a PR to the bench repo. draft of defs below — please critique:
"TTFT: wall time in ms from request acceptance to the first byte of the first token emitted by the model-serving runtime. Include queue/packing/kernel setup; exclude client-side network latency. Report median, p95, p99."
"TPOT: average time in ms between consecutive output tokens once streaming begins; report mean and 98th percentile. Use token boundary timestamps from runtime emitter."
"Goodput: tokens/sec that were emitted and accepted by client (post-filter); excludes failed / aborted requests. Use runtime counters for emitted tokens and measured wall time."
jen: nit: TPOT should be token-weighted avg, since variable token sizes matter less than time.
liam: and goodput should also clarify whether it's raw tokens or semantic tokens (we use model tokenization) — include both raw and normalized tokens.
maria: good catch. sasha, update defs accordingly.
perf-bot: loadtest summary — run_id=2026-02-12-09:12, mode=replay-24h, kernels=pinned-q8, avg_TTFT_median=42ms, p95_TTFT=118ms, p99_TTFT=310ms, avg_TPOT_warm=46ms, avg_TPOT_cold=82ms, goodput_ratio_warm_vs_cold=2.3
sasha: bot numbers look consistent with our notes. I'll include the bot CSV in the PR.
jen: are we comfortable labeling the synthetic burst as an "edge case" or must we standardize it into the canonical load profiles?
kai: we should standardize. create a Burst-ShortPrompt profile vs Steady-LongPrompt profile. both should be in the bench harness.
liam: final ask: when you open the PR, include a short reproducible command for running the harness and the relevant config snippet. e.g.:

bench_runner --mode=replay --trace=20260211-prod-trace.json --kernels=pinned-q8 --profile=Burst-ShortPrompt

maria: ok assigning chores: jen=metrics histograms, kai=local repro + trace dump, sasha=defs + PR, liam=cost/opt analysis notes. I'll review PR end of day tomorrow.
jen: ack :thumbsup:
kai: ack
sasha: ack, PR is incoming soon.
liam: thanks team.
maria: thanks! we'll iterate after the PR review.
